newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -Gilts look to budget for inspiration.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -Gilts look to budget for inspiration.

text.p: British gilts are pinning their hopes on the July budget to rescue them from their recent poor performance within Europe, analysts said on Wednesday.
The market suffered after the latest evidence of strong British economic growth sparked expectations of a two pronged monetary and fiscal attack by the authorities on inflation.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown is due to present his budget on July 2, and a half point rise in base rates at the next Bank of England monetary policy committee meeting on July 9-10 has been largely priced in.
"The second of July is the be all and end all," said Huw Roberts, European bond strategist at NatWest Capital Markets in London.
"If we get a fiscal statement that doesn't do enough to tighten policy then we will have to see more rate hikes, in which case we are going to see further flattening of the curve and even inversion."
Ian Amstad, senior economist at Bankers Trust in London, also said it was uncertain how many more interest rate increases would be needed to curb inflation.

"The short end is under continued pressure as the market looks for more rate rises, so I would steer clear," he said. "The long end is quite a safe-haven. You might suffer from an inverted yield curve and some negative carry but in the long run the new framework is going to deliver low inflation."
Amstad said base rates would be raised to whatever level was necessary to secure the inflation objective.
John McNeill, bond strategist at I.D.E.A. in London was more positive for gilts further out.
He said recent economic data had knocked gilts and the market was treading water for now.

"Gilts are near their worst levels at the moment and are quite soberly priced. The chances are that they will improve after the budget," he said. "At these levels a lot of bad news is priced in already."
He said with a neutral to slightly restrictive budget and a rate tightening in July the market's fears about inflation would start to subside and gilts would improve on a relative basis.
"Over the next couple of months gilts should start to benefit from the idea that the authorities have got on top of the problem and the fundamental background is good," he said.

McNeill said at its current level of 150 to 160 basis points the 10-year yield spread over Bunds offered a conservative valuation of gilts. He saw the gap narrowing to 125 to 120 on a two to three month scenario.

At 1109 GMT, the gilt/Bund gap was at 156 basis points having been at 185 at the beginning of the year and narrowing to 134 after the Bank of England was given independence to set interest rates in early May.
Roberts was more cautious saying it all depended on the colour of the budget.
"I don't see why we couldn't come in about 10 or 20 basis points. About 140 would be the first target," he said.
Analysts said Britain's position as a safe haven from European economic and monetary union had had more affect on sterling than it had on the gilt market.
"UK interest rates are already high by world standards and if they are going up even further sterling is very attractive," said McNeill.
"But it is not going to translate into the buying of gilts until there is a degree of comfort that the threat of serious deterioration in inflation is answered."
